mainTopic: Blood and meat flavor absorbed by utensils and food: roasting liver, the שחיטה knife, the salting bowl, the radish, and fish in a meat bowl eaten with כותח
overview: The amud opens with רב אשי criticizing a sage who roasted liver above meat. The חכמים allowed that only דיעבד, not לכתחילה. If a pan catches the drippings, even meat above liver is forbidden, because liver blood floats in the fat, while meat blood sinks. שמואל then rules that a knife used for שחיטה may not cut hot food, and that hot food may not be eaten from a bowl in which meat was salted, because מליח הרי הוא כרותח. רבין reports that רבי יוחנן disagrees, but אביי proves from רבי אמי's broken bowl that the report is wrong. רב כהנא allows a radish cut with a meat knife to be eaten with כותח, and אביי and רבא debate why it differs from the salting bowl, ending with whether the food can be tasted. Next, רב and שמואל argue about hot fish placed in a meat bowl: is second-hand flavor (נותן טעם בר נותן טעם) enough to forbid it with כותח? Stories about רב, שמואל, and two sages at the סורא ford follow. The final הלכה, from אביי, is that the fish is permitted with כותח but the radish is forbidden, and the גמרא begins to explain why the radish is special.

steps.title: רב אשי criticizes roasting liver above meat
steps.stepSummary: A sage roasts liver on a spit above meat. רב אשי calls him haughty, because the permission was only given דיעבד.
steps.simpleTranslation: He was skewering liver above meat. רב אשי said: How haughty is this sage! Say the Rabbis allowed it after the fact. Did they say it is allowed from the start?
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues: a sage puts liver above meat on the spit, and רב אשי criticizes him for doing this on purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Liver is full of blood, so when it sits on top, its blood drips onto the meat below. The חכמים only said such meat may be eaten if it already happened (דיעבד). Choosing to do it from the start (לכתחילה) treats a בדיעבד leniency as if it were a first choice, which רב אשי sees as arrogance.

keyTerms.meaning: After the fact, once it already happened
From the start, as a first choice

steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי is not saying the meat is forbidden. He agrees it may be eaten after the fact. His complaint is about doing it on purpose from the start.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic example of the difference between לכתחילה and דיעבד. Something can be fine once it has happened, yet still not be allowed as a first choice.

phrases.english: skewering liver on top of meat,
He (Rav Ashi) said: How haughty is this one of the Sages!
Say that the Sages said it is permitted after the fact,
did they say it is permitted from the start?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story and the discussion of roasting liver with meat from the previous lines.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Roasting liver above meat is permitted only דיעבד, not לכתחילה.

steps.title: With a drippings pan, even meat above liver is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: If a pan sits under the spit to catch drippings, even putting the meat above the liver is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if there is a pan for the drippings, then even meat on top of liver is also forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a new case: a pan sits under the spit to catch the drippings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, meat on top of liver is fine, because the liver's blood drips downward, away from the meat. With a pan below, the liver's blood falls into the fat that collects there, and a person may come to eat that mixture. So the problem is no longer the meat itself but the fat in the pan.

keyTerms.meaning: A pan or vessel under the spit that catches dripping fat

phrases.english: And if there is a pan for drippings,
meat on top of liver is also forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a stricter case to the roasting rules discussed in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When drippings collect in a pan, roasting meat and liver together is forbidden in any order.

steps.title: Why is meat blood in the pan any different?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rule: meat by itself also drips blood into the pan, yet that is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how is this different from the blood of meat?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question that challenges step 2, and it sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If roasting plain meat over a drippings pan is allowed, its blood also mixes with the fat. So why should liver blood in the pan forbid everything? The challenge says both cases look the same.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference? (asks why two cases that seem alike are treated differently)

phrases.english: And what is different from the blood of meat?
phrases.notes: He means plain meat roasting over the pan, which drips blood too and is allowed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule just stated in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a drippings pan forbids roasting meat and liver together
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Plain meat also drips blood into the pan and is permitted, so liver blood should be no worse.

steps.title: Meat blood sinks, liver blood floats
steps.stepSummary: Meat blood sinks below the fat, so the fat can be taken off. Liver blood floats in the fat and cannot be separated.
steps.simpleTranslation: Blood of meat sinks; blood of liver floats.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by pointing to a physical difference between the two kinds of blood.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Meat blood settles at the bottom of the pan, so the fat on top can be skimmed off clean. Liver blood rises and stays mixed in the fat, so it cannot be removed, and the whole mixture becomes forbidden.
steps.whatToRemember: A drippings pan makes roasting liver with meat forbidden in any order, because liver blood floats in the fat and cannot be separated. Meat blood sinks, so the fat can be saved.

phrases.english: The blood of meat sinks,
the blood of liver floats.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All blood dripping into the pan is the same, so liver blood should be treated like meat blood.
steps.terutzMaskana: Meat blood sinks and can be separated from the fat; liver blood floats and stays mixed in, so it forbids the fat.

steps.title: A knife used for slaughter and hot or cold food
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that a knife used for שחיטה may not cut hot food. For cold food there are two versions about whether rinsing is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: A knife used to slaughter may not be used to cut hot food. For cold food, some say the piece needs rinsing, and some say it does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: what a knife used for שחיטה may then be used to cut.
steps.deeperAnalysis: During שחיטה the knife takes in blood. Hot food would draw that blood out of the knife into itself, so cutting hot food is forbidden. With cold food nothing is absorbed, so the only question is blood resting on the surface. One version says the cut piece must be rinsed, and the other says even rinsing is not needed.

keyTerms.meaning: A knife that was used for שחיטה

steps.confusionAlert: The two versions only argue about cold food. Both agree that cutting hot food with this knife is forbidden.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said that Shmuel said:
A knife with which one slaughtered,
it is forbidden to cut boiling-hot food with it.
Cold food: some say it requires rinsing,
and some say it does not require rinsing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל סַכִּין שֶׁשָּׁחַט בָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new topic, still about blood mixing into food.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A knife used for שחיטה may not cut hot food. For cold food, there are two versions about whether the cut piece needs rinsing.

steps.title: A bowl used for salting meat may not be used for hot food
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that hot food may not be eaten from a bowl in which meat was salted. This follows his view that salted is like boiling and soaked is like cooked.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: If meat was salted in a bowl, you may not eat hot food in that bowl. שמואל is consistent here, because he holds that something salted acts like something boiling, and something soaked acts like something cooked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another rule from שמואל: a bowl used for salting meat may not be used for hot food. It then shows that this rule comes from a bigger principle שמואל holds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Salting meat draws blood out of it, and שמואל holds that salt acts like heat, so the bowl soaks up that blood. Hot food placed in the bowl afterward would take the blood back out. The line ושמואל לטעמיה shows that the bowl rule rests on שמואל's general principle that מליח is like רותח.

keyTerms.meaning: Something soaked or pickled in liquid for a long time
Following his own reasoning (he is being consistent)

steps.whyThisMatters: The principle מליח הרי הוא כרותח, that salting acts like heat, is the base for the הלכות of salting meat to remove its blood.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
A bowl in which one salted meat,
it is forbidden to eat boiling food in it,
and Shmuel follows his own reasoning,
for Shmuel said:
Something salted is like something boiling,
and something soaked is like something cooked.
phrases.notes: כבוש means food left soaking in a liquid like vinegar or brine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of שמואל's rules about utensils and meat, moving from the שחיטה knife to a salting bowl.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bowl in which meat was salted may not be used for hot food, because salted is like boiling (מליח הרי הוא כרותח).

steps.title: רבין reports that רבי יוחנן says salting is not like heat
steps.stepSummary: רבין brings a teaching in the name of רבי יוחנן that disagrees with שמואל: salted is not like boiling, and soaked is not like cooked.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבין came from ארץ ישראל, he said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Something salted is not like something boiling, and something soaked is not like something cooked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings an opposing report: רבין quotes רבי יוחנן as saying the exact opposite of שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If this report is right, salting a piece of meat would not make the bowl absorb blood, so the bowl could be used for hot food. This sets up a direct clash with שמואל's principle, which אביי will deal with in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: When he came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל, bringing a teaching)

phrases.english: When Ravin came,
he said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Something salted is not like something boiling,
and something soaked is not like something cooked.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רָבִין, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents an opposing opinion to the principle שמואל used in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבין's report, רבי יוחנן holds that salted is not like boiling and soaked is not like cooked.

steps.title: אביי rejects רבין's report using רבי אמי's broken bowl
steps.stepSummary: אביי says רבין's report is wrong. רבי אמי, a student of רבי יוחנן, broke a bowl that had been used for salting meat, which shows that רבי יוחנן holds salted is like boiling.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: רבין's report is not correct. In רבי אמי's house there was a bowl in which meat was salted, and he broke it. רבי אמי was a student of רבי יוחנן. Why would he break it? Surely because he heard רבי יוחנן say that salted is like boiling!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי rejects רבין's version of רבי יוחנן's teaching. He proves his point from something רבי אמי did.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Breaking a bowl only makes sense if salting made it absorb forbidden blood, which means salted is like boiling. Since רבי אמי learned from רבי יוחנן, his action shows what רבי יוחנן really taught. So רבי יוחנן agrees with שמואל, and רבין's report must be a mistake.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not so (this report is rejected)
Now, after all (introduces a known fact used to make a point)
Is it not because...? (a question that really means 'surely it is because')

steps.confusionAlert: אביי is not arguing against רבי יוחנן. He is saying רבין quoted רבי יוחנן wrongly, and that רבי יוחנן actually agrees with שמואל.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
This report of Ravin is not correct,

phrases.aramaic: דְּהַהִיא פִּינְכָּא דַּהֲוָה בֵּי רַבִּי אַמֵּי,
phrases.english: for there was a certain bowl in Rabbi Ami's house,
in which meat was salted,
and he broke it.

phrases.aramaic: מִכְּדֵי, רַבִּי אַמֵּי תַּלְמִיד דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הֲוָה,
phrases.english: Now, Rabbi Ami was a student of Rabbi Yochanan;
what is the reason he broke it?

phrases.aramaic: לָאו מִשּׁוּם דִּשְׁמִיעָא לֵיהּ מִינֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
phrases.english: Is it not because he heard from Rabbi Yochanan
who said: Something salted is like something boiling!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the report in step 7 and so supports שמואל's principle from step 6.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole report of רבין in the name of רבי יוחנן.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It goes against what רבי אמי, a student of רבי יוחנן, did, which shows רבי יוחנן holds מליח הרי הוא כרותח.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יוחנן holds salted is like boiling.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אמי broke a bowl in which meat had been salted.

steps.title: רב כהנא: salting bowl is forbidden, but a radish cut with a meat knife is allowed with milk
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא repeats that a bowl used for salting meat may not be used for hot food. He adds that a radish cut with a meat knife may be eaten with כותח, a milk dip.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא, the brother of רב יהודה, sat before רב הונא and said: A bowl in which meat was salted may not be used for hot food. But a radish cut with a meat knife may be eaten with כותח.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא gives two rulings side by side. One is strict (the salting bowl) and one is lenient (the radish).
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sharp radish pulls in some of the meat taste from the knife, much like salt pulls out blood, yet רב כהנא allows it with milk. Putting the two rulings next to each other raises a question: why is one forbidden and the other allowed? The גמרא asks this next.

keyTerms.meaning: A knife (here, one used for meat)
Before him (in front of a teacher)

phrases.aramaic: יָתֵיב רַב כָּהֲנָא אֲחוּהּ דְּרַב יְהוּדָה
phrases.english: Rav Kahana, the brother of Rav Yehuda, sat
before Rav Huna,
and he sat and said:
A bowl in which meat was salted —
it is forbidden to eat boiling food in it,
and a radish that one cut with a knife —
phrases.notes: He means a knife used for meat.

phrases.english: it is permitted to eat it with kutach.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָתֵיב רַב כָּהֲנָא אֲחוּהּ דְּרַב יְהוּדָה קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the salting bowl rule from step 6 and adds a lenient case to compare with it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A salting bowl is forbidden for hot food, but a radish cut with a meat knife may be eaten with a milk dip.

steps.title: What is the reason for the difference?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the salting bowl is forbidden while the radish is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רב כהנא's two rulings. This question sets up אביי's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases something soaks up taste: the bowl from the salted meat, and the radish from the meat knife. So why should the results be different? The question is looking for the line that separates the two cases.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
phrases.notes: He means: why is the bowl forbidden while the radish is allowed?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the two different rulings in step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the salting bowl is forbidden but the radish cut with a meat knife is allowed with milk.

steps.title: The radish absorbed something permitted; the bowl absorbed something forbidden
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the radish absorbed permitted meat fat, while the bowl absorbed forbidden blood.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: This one (the radish) absorbed something permitted, and that one (the bowl) absorbed something forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question. The difference is in what was absorbed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fat on a meat knife is kosher food in its own right, so a little meat taste in the radish is treated more lightly with milk. The salting bowl soaked up blood, which is forbidden by itself, so hot food in that bowl would take in something forbidden.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
This one absorbed something permitted,
phrases.notes: This one is the radish. It took in fat from the knife, and that fat is kosher to eat by itself.

phrases.english: and that one absorbed something forbidden.
phrases.notes: That one is the salting bowl, which soaked up blood.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The radish absorbed permitted fat, but the bowl absorbed forbidden blood.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: אביי's first answer is that the difference depends on whether the absorbed substance is permitted or forbidden by itself. רבא rejects this in the next step.

steps.title: רבא rejects אביי's answer about the radish
steps.stepSummary: רבא argues that the radish's meat fat being permitted does not help, because once it is eaten with כותח it becomes meat and milk.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: So what if the radish absorbed something permitted? In the end, this permitted thing leads to a prohibition, because the person is eating something forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא knocks down אביי's answer from the last step. He says the 'permitted fat' idea does not explain why the radish is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי said the radish is fine because it absorbed permitted meat fat, not forbidden blood. רבא points out that meat fat is permitted only when eaten alone. Once the radish is eaten with the milk dip, it becomes meat with milk, which is forbidden.

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
phrases.notes: He is answering אביי from the step before.

phrases.english: If it absorbed something permitted, what of it?
In the end, this permitted thing
is one that leads to a prohibition,
phrases.notes: Meat fat is fine alone, but with the milk dip it becomes meat and milk.

phrases.english: because he is eating something forbidden!

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי בָּלַע הֶיתֵּרָא, מַאי הָוֵי? סוֹף סוֹף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects אביי's answer in step 11.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: אביי's distinction between permitted fat and forbidden blood
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The meat fat becomes forbidden once it is eaten with milk, so 'permitted' does not explain the leniency.

steps.title: רבא's answer: the radish can be tasted, the bowl cannot
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains the difference: you can taste the radish to check for meat flavor, but you cannot taste the bowl's food to check for blood.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: This one (the radish) can be tasted, and that one (the bowl) cannot be tasted.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his own answer to the question from step 10.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A Jew may taste the radish before eating it with כותח, because meat flavor alone is permitted, so he can check whether it picked up a meat taste. He cannot taste food from the salting bowl, since that might mean tasting forbidden blood. That is why the bowl is treated strictly.

keyTerms.meaning: rather (drops the earlier answer and offers a new one)
it is possible to taste it

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
This one can be tasted,
phrases.notes: The radish: a Jew can taste it to check for meat flavor.

phrases.english: and that one cannot be tasted.
phrases.notes: The bowl: you can't test for blood by tasting, since blood is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces אביי's rejected answer with a new one.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New distinction based on whether a tasting check is possible
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The difference is permitted fat versus forbidden blood.
steps.terutzMaskana: The difference is that the radish can be tasted and the bowl's contents cannot.

steps.title: רב פפא asks: let a non-Jewish cook taste it
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא challenges רבא: the bowl's contents can be checked by a non-Jewish cook.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to רבא: But let a non-Jewish cook taste it!
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא attacks רבא's answer. He says there is a way to taste the bowl's food after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's answer depends on the bowl's food being impossible to taste. רב פפא points out that a non-Jewish cook, who may eat blood, could taste it and say whether there is a blood flavor. If so, the bowl should not be stricter than the radish.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to Rava:
But let a non-Jewish cook taste it,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's answer in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that the bowl's contents cannot be tasted
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A non-Jewish cook can taste it, so tasting is possible after all.

steps.title: רב פפא's support: רבא himself said a cook can taste
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא backs up his challenge with a teaching about a pot used for meat and milk or for תרומה, where רבא himself said a non-Jewish cook can taste.
steps.simpleTranslation: Didn't we learn: A pot in which meat was cooked should not be used for milk, and if it was, it depends on whether the meat gives taste. A pot in which תרומה was cooked should not be used for ordinary food, and if it was, it depends on whether the תרומה gives taste. And we asked: For תרומה, a כהן can taste it, but for meat and milk, who can taste it? And you told us: Let a cook taste it! So here too, let a cook taste it!
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא brings proof for his challenge from a teaching and from something רבא said before. He is turning רבא's own words against him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The teaching says the food is forbidden only if it picks up a taste, so someone must be able to taste it. For תרומה a כהן can taste, but for meat and milk no Jew can, and רבא himself answered: let a non-Jewish cook taste it. So the same solution should work for the salting bowl.

keyTerms.meaning: gives taste (the forbidden item counts only if its flavor is noticeable)
the portion given to a כהן, forbidden to non-כהנים

phrases.english: Didn't we learn:
A pot in which one cooked meat
one should not cook milk in it,
and if he cooked, it depends on whether it gives taste;
if he cooked teruma in it,
he should not cook ordinary food in it,
and if he cooked, it depends on whether it gives taste.
And we said:
Granted, teruma: a priest can taste it,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא בָּשָׂר בְּחָלָב – מַאן טָעֵים לַהּ?
phrases.english: but meat in milk: who can taste it?
And you told us: Let a cook taste it!
phrases.notes: "You" is רבא himself.

phrases.english: Here too, let a cook taste it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source behind רב פפא's challenge in step 14.
steps.raayaObject: That a non-Jewish cook's tasting counts as a valid check
steps.raayaSupportSource: The teaching about a pot used for meat or תרומה, together with רבא's own earlier ruling that a cook may taste

steps.title: רבא: I meant when no cook is available
steps.stepSummary: רבא agrees that a non-Jewish cook could taste, and limits his rule to a case where there is no such cook.
steps.simpleTranslation: Indeed so. When I said it, I meant a case where there is no cook.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers רב פפא by agreeing with him and narrowing his own statement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא does not take back his distinction. He says the bowl is forbidden only when no non-Jewish cook is around to taste. If a cook is available, the bowl's food could be checked just like the radish.
steps.whatToRemember: רבא's final distinction: the radish can always be tasted by a Jew, but the salting bowl's food can be checked only by a non-Jewish cook, so it is forbidden when no such cook is available.

phrases.english: Indeed so,
when I said it, it was where there is no cook.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב פפא's challenge by limiting the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא's rule seemed to apply even when a non-Jewish cook could taste.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule applies only where no non-Jewish cook is available.

steps.title: Hot fish in a meat bowl: רב and שמואל disagree
steps.stepSummary: A new dispute: hot fish placed in a meat bowl. רב forbids eating it with כותח, and שמואל permits it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: Fish that were put into a bowl: רב said it is forbidden to eat them with כותח, and שמואל said it is permitted to eat them with כותח.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a dispute between רב and שמואל about fish that touched a meat bowl.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hot fish were placed in a bowl that had been used for meat, so the fish may have picked up some meat taste. רב says that is enough to forbid eating it with a milk dip. שמואל says it is still permitted.

phrases.english: It was stated:
Fish that were put into a bowl,
phrases.notes: Hot fish placed in a bowl used for meat.

phrases.english: Rav said:
It is forbidden to eat them with kutach,
And Shmuel said:
It is permitted to eat them with kutach.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new related topic about absorbed meat taste and milk.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב forbids eating fish from a meat bowl with כותח, and שמואל permits it.

steps.title: The reasons behind רב and שמואל's dispute
steps.stepSummary: רב forbids because the fish holds real meat flavor. שמואל permits because the flavor is only second-hand, from the meat to the bowl to the fish.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב says it is forbidden, because the fish got real flavor. שמואל says it is permitted, because it is only flavor that came from flavor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the reason for each side of the fish-in-a-meat-bowl dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both agree the meat flavor passed from the bowl into the fish. רב says this still counts as real flavor, so the fish may not be eaten with dairy. שמואל says the flavor came in two steps, meat to bowl and bowl to fish, so it is too weak to count.

keyTerms.meaning: Imparted flavor: one food gives its taste to another
Flavor that came from flavor: taste passed along a second time, so it is weaker

steps.whatToRemember: רב: second-hand flavor still counts (forbidden). שמואל: second-hand flavor does not count (permitted).
steps.confusionAlert: שמואל does not say the fish got no taste from the bowl. He agrees it did. He only says that taste is too far removed from the meat to matter.
steps.whyThisMatters: The idea of נותן טעם בר נותן טעם is a key principle in the laws of meat and milk.

phrases.english: Rav says: it is prohibited,
it is a case of imparted flavor;
and Shmuel says: it is permitted,

phrases.aramaic: נוֹתֵן טַעַם בַּר נוֹתֵן טַעַם הוּא.
phrases.english: it is imparted flavor that comes from imparted flavor.

steps.triggerLanguage: רב אמר אסור נותן טעם הוא ושמואל אמר מותר נותן טעם בר נותן טעם הוא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning behind the rulings stated in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: the fish is forbidden with dairy because it holds meat flavor. שמואל: it is permitted because the flavor is only second-hand.

steps.title: רב's view was learned from a story about an eye ointment
steps.stepSummary: רב never said this ruling outright. People inferred it from a time he tasted ointment flavor in food cooked in a bowl that had held the ointment.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב's ruling was not said directly. It was figured out from a story: at his grandson's house, food put in a bowl that had held eye ointment tasted of the ointment, and רב said, 'It gives off so much taste!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says רב's opinion was not stated outright. It tells the story it was inferred from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ointment flavored the bowl, and the bowl then flavored the food. That is exactly second-hand flavor. Since רב tasted it clearly, people concluded that he holds second-hand flavor is strong enough to count.

keyTerms.meaning: By inference, figured out from something else

phrases.english: And this ruling of Rav was not stated explicitly,
rather, it was stated by inference.
For Rav happened to come to the house of

phrases.aramaic: רַב שִׁימִי בַּר חִיָּיא בַּר בְּרֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Rav Shimi bar Chiyya, his grandson,
he felt pain in his eyes,
phrases.notes: Both words mean 'in his eyes.' Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected, Aramaic way of saying it.

phrases.english: they made him an ointment in a clay bowl,

phrases.aramaic: בָּתַר הָכִי רְמוֹ לֵיהּ בִּשּׁוּלָא בְּגַוַּוהּ,
phrases.english: afterward they placed a cooked dish for him in it,
he tasted the flavor of the ointment in it,
he said: It gives off this much flavor!
phrases.notes: From this, people figured that רב holds second-hand flavor still counts.

steps.triggerLanguage: והא דרב לאו בפירוש איתמר אלא מכללא איתמר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains where רב's opinion from step 18 comes from.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב's ruling was inferred from his comment that ointment flavor came through strongly from a bowl into food.

steps.title: The ointment story does not prove anything
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the inference: the ointment was very bitter, so its strong taste passing along does not show that ordinary flavors do.
steps.simpleTranslation: But that is not right. That case is different, because the ointment was extremely bitter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the inference it just reported.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A very bitter substance is unusually strong, so even second-hand it can still be tasted. Meat flavor is not like that. So the story cannot teach us that רב forbids ordinary second-hand flavor.

keyTerms.meaning: But that is not so: a rejection of what was just said

steps.whyThisMatters: It weakens the basis for רב's opinion, since the only source for it turns out to be a special case.

phrases.english: But that is not so,
it is different there, because its bitterness was very great.

steps.triggerLanguage: ולא היא שאני התם דנפיש מרריה טפי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference drawn from the story in step 19.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that רב forbids second-hand flavor, drawn from the ointment story.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ointment was extremely bitter, so its strength is not typical of ordinary flavors like meat.

steps.title: שמואל says רב himself ate such fish
steps.stepSummary: שמואל ate fish from a meat bowl with כותח and offered some to רבי אלעזר, who refused. שמואל said that רב, רבי אלעזר's teacher, had eaten it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר stood before שמואל. They brought שמואל fish that had been put in a meat bowl, and he ate it with כותח. He offered some to רבי אלעזר, who did not eat. שמואל said: I gave this to your teacher and he ate, and you won't?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story in which שמואל claims that רב himself ate this kind of fish with dairy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר refuses because he follows רב, who forbids this. שמואל answers that רב himself ate it. That would suggest רב does not really forbid it.

keyTerms.meaning: Fish that were put into a bowl (one that had held meat)
A dip or relish made with milk

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar was standing
before Mar Shmuel,
they brought before him fish that had been put into a bowl,
and he was eating it with kutach.
He gave him some, and he did not eat,
phrases.notes: שמואל offered it to רבי אלעזר, and רבי אלעזר refused.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לְרַבָּךְ יְהַבִי לֵיהּ וַאֲכַל,
phrases.english: He said to him: I gave it to your teacher and he ate,
and you do not eat?

steps.triggerLanguage: רבי אלעזר הוה קאים קמיה דמר שמואל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the source of רב's opinion to a story suggesting רב acted against it.
steps.raayaObject: That רב does not really forbid fish from a meat bowl with dairy.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל's claim that he served such fish to רב and רב ate it.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר asks רב if he changed his mind
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר goes to רב and asks whether he has taken back his ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: He came before רב and said to him: Has the master taken back his ruling?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר checks with רב directly. His question sets up רב's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If שמואל's report is true, רב must have changed his mind. רבי אלעזר asks to find out whether רב still forbids this.

phrases.english: He came before Rav,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הֲדַר בֵּיהּ מָר מִשְּׁמַעְתֵּיהּ?
phrases.english: he said to him: Has the master taken back his ruling?

steps.triggerLanguage: אתא לקמיה דרב אמר ליה הדר ביה מר משמעתיה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on שמואל's claim in step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רב has changed his ruling and now permits fish from a meat bowl with dairy.

steps.title: רב denies ever eating it
steps.stepSummary: רב says שמואל would never feed him something he holds forbidden. So the claim is untrue and רב keeps his ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Heaven forbid that the son of אבא בר אבא would feed me something I do not hold is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers that he never ate such fish, so he has not changed his mind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב says שמואל would never serve him food that goes against רב's own view. So the report in step 21 cannot be true, and רב still forbids the fish with dairy.

keyTerms.meaning: I hold, it is my opinion

steps.whatToRemember: רב keeps his ruling: fish from a meat bowl may not be eaten with dairy. The story about him eating it is denied.

phrases.english: He said to him: Heaven forbid
for the offspring of Abba bar Abba
phrases.notes: This is שמואל. His father was אבא בר אבא.

phrases.aramaic: דְּלִיסְפֵּי לִי מִידֵּי וְלָא סְבִירָא לִי.
phrases.english: to feed me something that I do not hold.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר ליה חס ליה לזרעיה דאבא בר אבא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי אלעזר's question from step 22 and rejects שמואל's report from step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב did not change his mind. שמואל never fed him such fish.

steps.title: Two sages at the סורא ford: fish with כותח, and fruit without a ברכה
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא and רב חייא בר אשי sat on two sides of the סורא ford. One ate fish from a meat bowl with כותח. The other ate figs and grapes during the meal without a ברכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא and רב חייא בר אשי were sitting, one on each side of the סורא ford. One was brought fish that had been in a meat bowl and ate it with כותח. The other was brought figs and grapes during the meal, and he ate without making a ברכה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story of two sages and what each did. The fruit part seems to set up a new discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating the fish with כותח matches שמואל's lenient view. Eating figs and grapes during the meal without a separate ברכה raises a new question about blessings on fruit eaten during a meal.

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא וְרַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָשֵׁי הֲווֹ יָתְבִי,
phrases.english: Rav Huna and Rav Chiyya bar Ashi were sitting,
one on this side of the Sura ford,
and one on the other side of the ford.
phrases.notes: Literally it says 'this side' again, but it means the opposite side.

phrases.aramaic: לְמָר אַיְיתוֹ לֵיהּ דָּגִים שֶׁעָלוּ בַּקְּעָרָה
phrases.english: To one master they brought fish that had been put into a bowl
and he ate it with kutach,
to the other master they brought figs and grapes
during the meal,
and he ate and did not make a blessing.

steps.triggerLanguage: רב הונא ורב חייא בר אשי הוו יתבי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows sages following שמואל's lenient view on the fish, and opens a new topic about blessings during a meal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One sage ate fish from a meat bowl with כותח, and the other ate figs and grapes during the meal without a ברכה.

steps.title: Each sage challenges the other: would our teacher do this?
steps.stepSummary: Each of the two sages calls the other 'orphan' and asks whether their teacher would ever act this way.
steps.simpleTranslation: One sage said to the other: 'Orphan! Would your teacher do this?' And the other sage said back to him: 'Orphan! Would your teacher do this?'
steps.whatsHappening: Each sage objects to what the other is doing. One objects to eating fish from a meat bowl with כותח. The other objects to eating fruit during the meal without a ברכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling someone an 'orphan' is a sharp way of saying he acts like a student with no teacher to guide him. The question 'Would your teacher do this?' is really a challenge: each one says the other's behavior goes against the teacher they share.

keyTerms.meaning: Orphan; here, a student acting as if he had no teacher

phrases.english: One Sage said to his colleague:
phrases.notes: This is the one who saw his friend eating the fish with כותח.

phrases.english: Orphan! Would your teacher do this?
phrases.notes: 'Orphan' is a jab. He means: you act as if you never had a teacher.

phrases.english: And the other Sage said to his colleague:
Orphan! Would your teacher do this?
phrases.notes: This time the complaint is about eating the figs and grapes without a ברכה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story from step 24: each sage now objects to what the other did.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two lenient practices from step 24: fish from a meat bowl eaten with כותח, and fruit eaten during the meal without a ברכה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Their shared teacher would not act this way, so each student is acting against his own teacher's guidance.

steps.title: Each sage explains which authority he follows
steps.stepSummary: One says he follows שמואל on the fish. The other says he follows רבי חייא, who taught that bread and wine exempt other foods and drinks.
steps.simpleTranslation: One sage said: 'I hold like שמואל.' The other sage said: 'I hold like רבי חייא, because רבי חייא taught: Bread exempts all types of food, and wine exempts all types of drinks.'
steps.whatsHappening: Each sage defends himself by naming the authority he relies on. The one who ate the fish relies on שמואל. The one who ate fruit without a ברכה relies on a ברייתא of רבי חייא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither one claims his teacher would agree. Each says he chose to follow a different respected opinion. שמואל allows fish from a meat bowl with כותח (steps 17-18). רבי חייא teaches that the ברכה on bread covers every food in the meal, so the fruit needs no ברכה of its own.

keyTerms.meaning: I hold, this is my opinion
Bread exempts; the ברכה on bread covers other foods
Wine exempts; the ברכה on wine covers other drinks

phrases.english: One Sage said to his colleague:
I hold in accordance with Shmuel,
phrases.notes: This goes back to step 21, where שמואל ate fish from a meat bowl with כותח.

phrases.english: And the other Sage said to his colleague:
I hold in accordance with Rabbi Chiyya,
as Rabbi Chiyya teaches:
Bread exempts all types of food,
and wine exempts all types of drinks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenges of step 25.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why each sage acted against what their teacher would do.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Each one follows another authority: שמואל for the fish, and רבי חייא's ברייתא for the fruit.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a student may follow another accepted authority, even against his own teacher's practice.

steps.title: The final הלכה: fish in a meat bowl is allowed, a radish cut with a meat knife is not
steps.stepSummary: חזקיה quotes אביי: fish put in a meat bowl may be eaten with כותח, but a radish cut with a meat knife may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: חזקיה said in the name of אביי: The הלכה is that fish placed in a bowl may be eaten with כותח. A radish cut with a knife that was used to cut meat may not be eaten with כותח.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final ruling on the fish question and adds a ruling about a radish. Fish are allowed, but the radish is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the fish, the הלכה follows שמואל's lenient view from step 17, against רב. The radish ruling goes against רב כהנא's lenient statement in step 9: a radish cut with a meat knife may not be eaten with כותח. So the two cases get opposite results, even though both involve a meat utensil.

keyTerms.meaning: Fish that were placed into a (meat) bowl
A knife that was used to cut meat

steps.whatToRemember: Fish in a meat bowl may be eaten with כותח. A radish cut with a meat knife may not.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the two rulings contradict each other. The fish only sat in a bowl, while the radish was cut with a meat knife, and the גמרא treats the radish more strictly.

phrases.english: Chizkiya says in the name of Abaye:
The halakha is: fish that were placed into a bowl —
phrases.notes: The bowl here is one used for meat, as in the earlier stories.

phrases.english: it is permitted to eat them with kutach,
a radish that one cut with a knife
with which he had cut meat —
it is prohibited to eat it with kutach.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the stories and the arguments, the גמרא states the practical law.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Fish placed in a meat bowl may be eaten with כותח. A radish cut with a meat knife may not be eaten with כותח.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical ruling for a meat utensil that touches food later eaten with dairy.

steps.title: Setting up a limit: this applies only to a radish
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to limit אביי's strict ruling to a radish.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this statement applies only to a radish,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move: it starts to explain that the strict ruling about the knife applies only to a radish. The rest of the limit continues in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase והני מילי tells us that a limit on the ruling is coming. It narrows the strict ruling of step 27 so that it does not automatically apply to every food cut with a meat knife.

keyTerms.meaning: And these words apply only to...; introduces a limit on a ruling

phrases.english: And this statement applies only to a radish,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins to narrow the radish ruling from step 27.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The strict knife ruling is limited to a radish (the explanation continues in the next part of the text).
